caption:
Why did everyone leave Bodie, California?

Gold was found in the Bodie Hills in 1859, but the camp stayed small until the Standard Company hit a rich vein in 1876. By 1879 Bodie had about 2,000 buildings and 7,000–10,000 people, and 65 saloons along a mile of Main Street.

Decline began in 1880, as booms in Butte, Tombstone and Utah drew the single miners away. The 1890 fire insurance map gives the population as 450. The last newspaper printed in 1912. Bodie was first called a ghost town in 1915. The last mine closed in 1942 under War Production Board order L-208, which shut non-essential US gold mines during the war. Mining never resumed.

One thing Bodie did first: in 1892 the Standard Company built a hydroelectric plant 13 miles away and sent 3,530 volts to its 20-stamp mill — the country's first long-distance transmission of electricity.

Winters are brutal at 8,379 feet: an average 303 nights a year below freezing, a record low of −36°F, winds near 100 mph.

Today it is a state park held in "arrested decay" — about 110 structures, interiors still stocked with goods, china shards and square nails in the dirt. Removing them is illegal.

Still unresolved: the story of Rosa May, said to have nursed the town through an epidemic and then been buried outside the cemetery fence, is unsubstantiated. And the legend that Bodie was California's second or third largest city in 1880 is contradicted by that year's census.

Images: house and saloon interior by PDPhoto.org and Jon Sullivan, 2004; storefronts and boot by Dick Rowan, 1972, US National Archives; bird's-eye view by William Thompson, c.1890; Sanborn-Perris fire map, 1890, Library of Congress.
